Dr Sylvia Earle

By: Diana Lucas | Paid

Proposal


Show:

Summary:
Arguably the world’s most renowned ocean scientists and deep see explorer visiting the Southern Cape Coast in February?

‘It’s the blue heart of the planet, we should take care of our heart’

I am not sure where to begin with Sylvia Earle.
Scuba diver, oceanographer, marine biologist, aquanaut, lecturer, author, research scientist.

She’s 88 years old. She’s become an elder of ocean

Sylvia started scuba diving at University (studying marine biology). .Jacques Cousteau had just ‘invented’ the scuba suit and Sylvia and her tutor managed to get hold of one of the early prototypes. That first dive gave her the gift of time underwater and made her want to go deeper, stay longer. She was hooked.

For over 5 decades Sylvia has been a pioneer of deep water exploration and has remained at the forefront of research as a marine explorer.

In 1970, Sylvia, led a research team (Tektite II Project) where for two weeks they lived in an underwater habitat (about 15 metres), off the coast of the Virgin Isles. The researchers were able to study marine life continuously without having to surface. Sylvia went into the project as an ivory tower scientist but coming out everything changed. Honoured at the White House, a parade in Chicago, full on media attention.

‘I had to get out of my shell’

She made it her life’s work to share her passion for marine life with a wider audience.



Further information:
‘Sylvia Earle was a pioneer - invading the oceanographer bearded flannel shirt image –she became a public face for science’

Often referred to as ‘Her Deepness’ Dr Sylvia Earle holds the record for the deepest walk on the sea floor. Wearing a pressurized (JIM) suit she was carried to a depth of 1 250 feet (381 metres) where she detached from the submersible and explored the sea floor for two and a half hours. The first woman to walk the sea floor beyond 1000 feet (about 305 metres).

In the 1980’s she teamed up with engineer Graham Hawkes (who became her third husband), to design and build an underwater vehicle that helped scientists work at unprecedented depths. Graham talks about their initial conversation:

What I remember was Sylvia saying why can’t we go to the bottom of the ocean? I’d spent five years I think getting from 1 500 feet(458 metres) to 2000 feet (610m) and here is Sylvia saying I want to go to 37 000 feet (11 278) ….. and then I am thinking Lady I can tell you all sorts of reasons why we can’t do it and in the end I knocked those reasons down in my mind and I thought maybe we could…so Sylvia inspired me-that was the way that worked…’

Sylvia and Graham’s company Deep Ocean Exploration and Research Marine makes crewed subs, camera housings, grasping tools that scientists use to study ice in Antarctica and to film the fragile coral reefs. They designed a one-man deep water capsule (Deep Rover) for (Titanic director) James Cameron, to explore some of the deepest and inhospitable ocean depths. (They didn’t design the Titan capsule which tragically exploded in June last year).

James: ‘She broke through the barriers, one of the first female scientists to do this’

Sylvia Earle has ben a National Geographic explorer at large (formerly explorer in residence) since 1998.

First female chief scientist of the US National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration.

In 1998 Sylvia was named by Time Magazine as its first hero of the planet, in 2014 United Nations Champion of the Earth amongst many other awards and honours.

Sylvia has received more than 32 honorary degrees and has over 225 scientific and technical publications to her name.

Today, at the age of 88, she is one of the ocean’s best-known defenders - a blue water advocate who has seen the oceans change in her diving lifetime.

In 2011 she went back to St Johns, US Virgin Island, diving at the site of the Tektite project in 1970. The coral reef, that had been alive and full of marine life were no longer, the footage they shot shows a brown/grey lifeless reef with no fish. Stats show that from 1950 to 2014 there has been a 50% decline in coral reefs.

When Sylvia began exploring the ocean 50 years ago no one imagined that Earth’s vast expanse of water could be in any way harmed by what we put into or what we take out of it

It seemed, at that time, to be a sea of Eden, but now we know, and we are now facing paradise lost.

But things have changed with over fishing, industrial and other methods – like trawling the ocean floor, raking up vast quantities of marine life and in the process destroying vast amounts of what is called by-product. Oil drilling, dumping – these and more are causing coral reefs to die as the fish die (Their excretions nurture the coral reefs).

Over the years I have seen changes, I have been a witness to perhaps the greatest area of discovery about the ocean but at the same time the greatest area of loss.

Sylvia has spent her life advocating for ocean conservation and education about the role the sea plays in climate change.

We understand that leaving trees, or planting trees really helps the carbon equation but nothing matters more than maintaining the integrity of ocean systems. These big animals, even the little ones, they take up carbon, they sequester carbon when they sink to the bottom of the ocean. The ocean is the biggest carbon sink on the planet.

To this end in 2009 Sylvia founded Mission Blue, a nonprofit ocean advocacy group, dedicated to protecting the ocean from threats such as climate change, pollution, habitat destruction, invasive species, and dramatic decrease in ocean fish stocks.

Sylvia’s wish for the ocean is to protect the ocean as we protect – or try to protect - the land. Her idea is to develop areas ‘Hope Spots’, marine reserves. Working with, empowering and supporting individuals and communities around the world in their efforts to protect the ocean. It’s not just protecting pretty places but identifying the potential and the threats to an area and then take concrete action.

One of the first Hope Spots was in Cabo Pulmo, New Mexico, once a thriving fishing village. Then the sports fisherman came, then the industrial fleet with their long lines and nets by the 1980’s so much had been taken from the surrounding water that nothing was left. In 1997 the people who live there took the ocean back. Together they created a Hope Spot - 70 square kilometres - the Cabo Pulmo Marine reserve – making it completely off limits to fishing dumping and drilling. Since the protected zone was established Cabo Pulmo has replaced fishing with eco tourism and the community is thriving. Sylvia went diving and the visuals of the fish thriving in the sea are astounding.

They have designated six Hope Spots along the South African Coast: False Bay, Cape Whale Coast, Knysna, Plettenberg Bay, Algoa Bay and Aliwal Shoal. COVID paused their work in SA.

Sylvia will be here in early February to re-activate the Hope Spots. She will be in Cape Town and Plettenberg Bay. She will be working closely with the Nature’s Valley Trust in Plettenberg Bay and Knysna. She and her team will be holding workshops and bringing local stakeholders together who work in marine conservation.

I propose a profile on Sylvia, with the jumping off point the Plettenberg Bay Hope Spot, intertwined with her life. Using visuals and footage of her early life, scuba diving, key moments – I have requested this footage. I am waiting for some more detail on the Hope Spots which will be coming this week.

Sylvia is a wonderful interview, she wears her passion lightly, there is a joy in her voice, demeanor, always curious, never cynical, very engaging.

James Cameron calls her the Joan of Arc of the ocean, she’s the one that’s out in the front leading the charge in the fight to save the ocean. And she has made it her life’s purpose in the last couple of decades to make sure everyone else understands what’s going on and why it’s important.

Script:


V/O
Saturday morning and Long Beach, Simon’s Town is awash with swimmers, paddlers and even man’s best friend.

V/O
People who have come to welcome; to see; to acknowledge Sylvia Earle. GAP

For many she could be any retiree, a summer swallow here in South Africa to soak up the sun.

V/O
But in the world of marine research and ocean conservation 88 year-old, Dr Sylvia Earle is a rock star.

Sylvia: Very inspiring
Erin: Even the dog
Sylvia: Two dogs one plastic one real

Link: Called the Joan of Arc of the Ocean she’s leading the charge to save the seas.

V/O
A moment in time, Sylva calls it. A crossroads when communities and countries can join forces and play a role

TITLE
Dr Sylvia Earle
Marine Explorer and Scientist

Sylvia: 50 years ago we were not as aware as we are now. Aware of the changes of climate and the causes. 50 years from now it will be too late to do what we can do right now…lose a million species by the end of this century unless we take action right now.

LINK: Sylvia has been exploring, diving, researching the ocean for over six decades - one of the few who has seen how the sea has changed. A witness of what we can do to the natural world.

Sylvia: I wish all of you would use all means at your disposal to ignite public support for a global network of marine protected areas – Hope Spots

V/O
Sylvia’s wish has led to what she calls Hope Spots. While Marine protected areas are official designated zones enforced by legislation, Hope Spots are areas identified and driven by their communities, pressure groups bringing together the world’s best brains in marine biology.

V/O
There are now 159 Hope Spots around the world, and still counting……. False Bay here in the Western Cape is one of them.

Whale and Sylvia

V/O
Through her NGO Mission Blue, Sylvia and the team travel the world driving awareness on the urgency of saving the ocean. Workshops and conferences like this at Cape Town’s Two Oceans Aquarium foster ideas and motivate.

Link: Sylvia spends over 200 days of the year on the road, on planes, lobbying governments and inspiring people she says there is nothing she would rather be doing, that is out of the water.

Sylvia: I am just driven because I am aware of how much most people simply don’t know and you can’t care if you don’t know So I feel I can’t afford to be self indulgent and splash around.

V/O
Sylvia’s been splashing around for most of her 88 years…… Free diving off Florida’s coastline as a teenager, it was only as a student studying marine biology that Sylvia and her lecturer managed to get hold of one of the early prototypes of the scuba suit.

Sylvia: it was 1953, I had two words of instruction breathe naturally and over the side it was hard to come out of the water I wanted to stay.
Erin: Do you still feel that rush when you get into the ocean now?
Sylvia: Its like going home, VISUAL…BREAK that feeling of weightlessness and expectation you don’t know who you are going to see, who is going to be down there but always something, always one or lots of individuals just glad to have a chance to meet them.

Sylvia: Diving into the ocean is like diving into the history of life on earth. because you see a kingdom of life.

Link: She’s seen parts of the world we can’t imagine. And gone to depths thought impossible to reach.

Erin: So you amongst your many accolades hold a deep sea diving record?
Sylvia: Well I had the chance to use a system called JIM, named after the first person willing to put it on I was able to go to 400 metres. It was the deepest solo dive at the point. And then later going to 1000 metres, I was taken on the front end of a little submarine called the Star 2 in Hawaii and stepped off it connected only by a communication line to the submarine back to the surface.
Erin: What did that feel like?
To be able to walk on the ocean floor and to be a witness to see what was down there.

UP SOUND:
…attractive women

V/O
This might seem like a frivolous jaunt but’s that’s more to do with the media’s perception of women at the time. It was 1970 when Sylvia led the first all female team of aquanauts, marine researchers and scientists to live in an underwater habitat, off the coast of the Virgin Isles in the Caribbean.

Having the gift of time, to study the marine life continuously.

Sylvia: It was just so amazing – we were living warm and dry inside and underwater lab, microscopes and a hot shower a lot of things having all the comforts of home but its when we went outside that we really went home.

V/O
Fort- one years later, Sylvia returned to the same area. It was a different picture. Right in front of her eyes she saw the extent of the problem.

Sylvia: It was like a ghost town…. we’re talking 40 years that s rapid change to lose the abundance of life so fast.

V/O
Industrial and over fishing, dumping, pollution all destroying our seas. It’s Missions Blues goal to turn that around.

Sylvia: We are alive because the ocean is alive, It’s the living ocean that is now in trouble because of what we put into it…masses amounts of wildlife we have extracted, but knowing that we have the best chance to shift to say now understand and once you see you can’t un see.

V/O
The oceans absorb the greatest volume of Carbon dioxide and emit the greatest volume of oxygen compared to any eco system (on land) – and a healthy ocean keeps the earths climate in balance.

Up Sound Look at this its and ocean full of whale sharks

V/O
In South Africa 5% of our coastal waters are demarcated Marine Protected which is reasonably high compared to most other countries. enforcement however could be better.

V/O
Sometimes community activism is the difference between official neglect and effective marine protection. Recently the South African navy cancelled their planned underwater explosives training in Simonstown after a show of force from the community. An example of the muscle a Hope Spot can flex.

Sylvia: Nobody can do it all but everybody can do something it’s a team sport GO Team.
Erin: Go team.

V/O
Right now, 8% of the oceans around the world have some sort of Marine Protection…. Sylvia’s pushing for 30% by 2030. Extending marine protection to the High Seas, the areas of the oceans not controlled by any country.

Sylvia: If we can protect half the world, the blue half that is beyond national jurisdiction we can go along way we can go along way to stabilising climate, stabilising temperature, stabilise the loss of diversity. It’s the Blue Heart of the planet it’s where oxygen is generated where carbon is captured. The high seas is one of best chances we will ever, have right now.

Link: Sylvia spends over 200 days of the year on the road, on planes, lobbying governments and inspiring people she says there is nothing she would rather be doing, that is out of the water. Sylvia: I am just driven because I am aware of how much most people simply don’t know and you can’t care if you don’t know So I feel I can’t afford to be self indulgent and splash around. V/O Sylvia’s been splashing around for most of her 88 years…… Free diving off Florida’s coastline as a teenager, it was only as a student studying marine biology that Sylvia and her lecturer managed to get hold of one of the early prototypes of the scuba suit. Sylvia: it was 1953, I had two words of instruction breathe naturally and over the side it was hard to come out of the water I wanted to stay. Erin: Do you still feel that rush when you get into the ocean now? Sylvia: Its like going home, VISUAL…BREAK that feeling of weightlessness and expectation you don’t know who you are going to see, who is going to be down there but always something, always one or lots of individuals just glad to have a chance to meet them. Sylvia: Diving into the ocean is like diving into the history of life on earth. because you see a kingdom of life. Link: She’s seen parts of the world we can’t imagine. And gone to depths thought impossible to reach. Erin: So you amongst your many accolades hold a deep sea diving record? Sylvia: Well I had the chance to use a system called JIM, named after the first person willing to put it on I was able to go to 400 metres. It was the deepest solo dive at the point. And then later going to 1000 metres, I was taken on the front end of a little submarine called the Star 2 in Hawaii and stepped off it connected only by a communication line to the submarine back to the surface. Erin: What did that feel like? To be able to walk on the ocean floor and to be a witness to see what was down there. UP SOUND: …attractive women V/O This might seem like a frivolous jaunt but’s that’s more to do with the media’s perception of women at the time. It was 1970 when Sylvia led the first all female team of aquanauts, marine researchers and scientists to live in an underwater habitat, off the coast of the Virgin Isles in the Caribbean. Having the gift of time, to study the marine life continuously. Sylvia: It was just so amazing – we were living warm and dry inside and underwater lab, microscopes and a hot shower a lot of things having all the comforts of home but its when we went outside that we really went home. V/O Fort- one years later, Sylvia returned to the same area. It was a different picture. Right in front of her eyes she saw the extent of the problem. Sylvia: It was like a ghost town…. we’re talking 40 years that s rapid change to lose the abundance of life so fast. V/O Industrial and over fishing, dumping, pollution all destroying our seas. It’s Missions Blues goal to turn that around. Sylvia: We are alive because the ocean is alive, It’s the living ocean that is now in trouble because of what we put into it…masses amounts of wildlife we have extracted, but knowing that we have the best chance to shift to say now understand and once you see you can’t un see. V/O The oceans absorb the greatest volume of Carbon dioxide and emit the greatest volume of oxygen compared to any eco system (on land) – and a healthy ocean keeps the earths climate in balance. Up Sound Look at this its and ocean full of whale sharks V/O In South Africa 5% of our coastal waters are demarcated Marine Protected which is reasonably high compared to most other countries. enforcement however could be better. V/O Sometimes community activism is the difference between official neglect and effective marine protection. Recently the South African navy cancelled their planned underwater explosives training in Simonstown after a show of force from the community. An example of the muscle a Hope Spot can flex. Sylvia: Nobody can do it all but everybody can do something it’s a team sport GO Team. Erin: Go team. V/O Right now, 8% of the oceans around the world have some sort of Marine Protection…. Sylvia’s pushing for 30% by 2030. Extending marine protection to the High Seas, the areas of the oceans not controlled by any country. Sylvia: If we can protect half the world, the blue half that is beyond national jurisdiction we can go along way we can go along way to stabilising climate, stabilising temperature, stabilise the loss of diversity. It’s the Blue Heart of the planet it’s where oxygen is generated where carbon is captured. The high seas is one of best chances we will ever, have right now.

metadata.Summary: Arguably the world’s most renowned ocean scientists and deep see explorer visiting the Southern Cape Coast in February? ‘It’s the blue heart of the planet, we should take care of our heart’ I am not sure where to begin with Sylvia Earle. Scuba diver, oceanographer, marine biologist, aquanaut, lecturer, author, research scientist. She’s 88 years old. She’s become an elder of ocean Sylvia started scuba diving at University (studying marine biology). .Jacques Cousteau had just ‘invented’ the scuba suit and Sylvia and her tutor managed to get hold of one of the early prototypes. That first dive gave her the gift of time underwater and made her want to go deeper, stay longer. She was hooked. For over 5 decades Sylvia has been a pioneer of deep water exploration and has remained at the forefront of research as a marine explorer. In 1970, Sylvia, led a research team (Tektite II Project) where for two weeks they lived in an underwater habitat (about 15 metres), off the coast of the Virgin Isles. The researchers were able to study marine life continuously without having to surface. Sylvia went into the project as an ivory tower scientist but coming out everything changed. Honoured at the White House, a parade in Chicago, full on media attention. ‘I had to get out of my shell’ She made it her life’s work to share her passion for marine life with a wider audience.
metadata.Further information: ‘Sylvia Earle was a pioneer - invading the oceanographer bearded flannel shirt image –she became a public face for science’ Often referred to as ‘Her Deepness’ Dr Sylvia Earle holds the record for the deepest walk on the sea floor. Wearing a pressurized (JIM) suit she was carried to a depth of 1 250 feet (381 metres) where she detached from the submersible and explored the sea floor for two and a half hours. The first woman to walk the sea floor beyond 1000 feet (about 305 metres). In the 1980’s she teamed up with engineer Graham Hawkes (who became her third husband), to design and build an underwater vehicle that helped scientists work at unprecedented depths. Graham talks about their initial conversation: What I remember was Sylvia saying why can’t we go to the bottom of the ocean? I’d spent five years I think getting from 1 500 feet(458 metres) to 2000 feet (610m) and here is Sylvia saying I want to go to 37 000 feet (11 278) ….. and then I am thinking Lady I can tell you all sorts of reasons why we can’t do it and in the end I knocked those reasons down in my mind and I thought maybe we could…so Sylvia inspired me-that was the way that worked…’ Sylvia and Graham’s company Deep Ocean Exploration and Research Marine makes crewed subs, camera housings, grasping tools that scientists use to study ice in Antarctica and to film the fragile coral reefs. They designed a one-man deep water capsule (Deep Rover) for (Titanic director) James Cameron, to explore some of the deepest and inhospitable ocean depths. (They didn’t design the Titan capsule which tragically exploded in June last year). James: ‘She broke through the barriers, one of the first female scientists to do this’ Sylvia Earle has ben a National Geographic explorer at large (formerly explorer in residence) since 1998. First female chief scientist of the US National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration. In 1998 Sylvia was named by Time Magazine as its first hero of the planet, in 2014 United Nations Champion of the Earth amongst many other awards and honours. Sylvia has received more than 32 honorary degrees and has over 225 scientific and technical publications to her name. Today, at the age of 88, she is one of the ocean’s best-known defenders - a blue water advocate who has seen the oceans change in her diving lifetime. In 2011 she went back to St Johns, US Virgin Island, diving at the site of the Tektite project in 1970. The coral reef, that had been alive and full of marine life were no longer, the footage they shot shows a brown/grey lifeless reef with no fish. Stats show that from 1950 to 2014 there has been a 50% decline in coral reefs. When Sylvia began exploring the ocean 50 years ago no one imagined that Earth’s vast expanse of water could be in any way harmed by what we put into or what we take out of it It seemed, at that time, to be a sea of Eden, but now we know, and we are now facing paradise lost. But things have changed with over fishing, industrial and other methods – like trawling the ocean floor, raking up vast quantities of marine life and in the process destroying vast amounts of what is called by-product. Oil drilling, dumping – these and more are causing coral reefs to die as the fish die (Their excretions nurture the coral reefs). Over the years I have seen changes, I have been a witness to perhaps the greatest area of discovery about the ocean but at the same time the greatest area of loss. Sylvia has spent her life advocating for ocean conservation and education about the role the sea plays in climate change. We understand that leaving trees, or planting trees really helps the carbon equation but nothing matters more than maintaining the integrity of ocean systems. These big animals, even the little ones, they take up carbon, they sequester carbon when they sink to the bottom of the ocean. The ocean is the biggest carbon sink on the planet. To this end in 2009 Sylvia founded Mission Blue, a nonprofit ocean advocacy group, dedicated to protecting the ocean from threats such as climate change, pollution, habitat destruction, invasive species, and dramatic decrease in ocean fish stocks. Sylvia’s wish for the ocean is to protect the ocean as we protect – or try to protect - the land. Her idea is to develop areas ‘Hope Spots’, marine reserves. Working with, empowering and supporting individuals and communities around the world in their efforts to protect the ocean. It’s not just protecting pretty places but identifying the potential and the threats to an area and then take concrete action. One of the first Hope Spots was in Cabo Pulmo, New Mexico, once a thriving fishing village. Then the sports fisherman came, then the industrial fleet with their long lines and nets by the 1980’s so much had been taken from the surrounding water that nothing was left. In 1997 the people who live there took the ocean back. Together they created a Hope Spot - 70 square kilometres - the Cabo Pulmo Marine reserve – making it completely off limits to fishing dumping and drilling. Since the protected zone was established Cabo Pulmo has replaced fishing with eco tourism and the community is thriving. Sylvia went diving and the visuals of the fish thriving in the sea are astounding. They have designated six Hope Spots along the South African Coast: False Bay, Cape Whale Coast, Knysna, Plettenberg Bay, Algoa Bay and Aliwal Shoal. COVID paused their work in SA. Sylvia will be here in early February to re-activate the Hope Spots. She will be in Cape Town and Plettenberg Bay. She will be working closely with the Nature’s Valley Trust in Plettenberg Bay and Knysna. She and her team will be holding workshops and bringing local stakeholders together who work in marine conservation. I propose a profile on Sylvia, with the jumping off point the Plettenberg Bay Hope Spot, intertwined with her life. Using visuals and footage of her early life, scuba diving, key moments – I have requested this footage. I am waiting for some more detail on the Hope Spots which will be coming this week. Sylvia is a wonderful interview, she wears her passion lightly, there is a joy in her voice, demeanor, always curious, never cynical, very engaging. James Cameron calls her the Joan of Arc of the ocean, she’s the one that’s out in the front leading the charge in the fight to save the ocean. And she has made it her life’s purpose in the last couple of decades to make sure everyone else understands what’s going on and why it’s important.
